supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

supporting_evidence.text: Data_2 progression: speed, cadence, step length, and stride length: Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, distance-time gait parameters; Data_2 approximations documented by feature extraction)

Data_2 gait-cycle timing: swing, stance, double support, and asymmetry: Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, gait-cycle and stance/swing timing; Data_2 event definitions)

Data_2 biomechanical feature provenance and limits: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: clinical_gait_signals_2025 (Clinical Gait Signals paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Data_2 marks U-turn boundaries during the out-and-back walking protocol. A prolonged U-turn duration is a turning-performance finding and should be interpreted together with straight-walking speed, cadence, asymmetry, and support timing. It can suggest slower or less efficient turning, but it should not be converted into a diagnosis or fall-risk claim without additional validated evidence. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper; clinical gait-analysis review sources

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, distance-time gait parameters; Data_2 approximations documented by feature extraction)

Data_2 gait-cycle timing: swing, stance, double support, and asymmetry: Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, gait-cycle and stance/swing timing; Data_2 event definitions)

Data_2 biomechanical feature provenance and limits: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: clinical_gait_signals_2025 (Clinical Gait Signals paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, distance-time gait parameters; Data_2 approximations documented by feature extraction)

Data_2 gait-cycle timing: swing, stance, double support, and asymmetry: Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, gait-cycle and stance/swing timing; Data_2 event definitions)

Data_2 biomechanical feature provenance and limits: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: clinical_gait_signals_2025 (Clinical Gait Signals paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Data_2 marks U-turn boundaries during the out-and-back walking protocol. A prolonged U-turn duration is a turning-performance finding and should be interpreted together with straight-walking speed, cadence, asymmetry, and support timing. It can suggest slower or less efficient turning, but it should not be converted into a diagnosis or fall-risk claim without additional validated evidence. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper; clinical gait-analysis review sources

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

supporting_evidence.text: Data_2 progression: speed, cadence, step length, and stride length: Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, distance-time gait parameters; Data_2 approximations documented by feature extraction)

Data_2 gait-cycle timing: swing, stance, double support, and asymmetry: Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, gait-cycle and stance/swing timing; Data_2 event definitions)

Pathology-aware interpretation without diagnosis: The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: pathological_gait_local_review_set (PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md plus local PDFs)

Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Data_2 marks U-turn boundaries during the out-and-back walking protocol. A prolonged U-turn duration is a turning-performance finding and should be interpreted together with straight-walking speed, cadence, asymmetry, and support timing. It can suggest slower or less efficient turning, but it should not be converted into a diagnosis or fall-risk claim without additional validated evidence. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper; clinical gait-analysis review sources

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

supporting_evidence.text: The Clinical Gait Signals dataset provides wearable IMU trials with detected toe-off and heel-strike events, U-turn boundaries, sampling frequency, cohort labels, pathology labels, visual gait assessment, and pathology-specific clinical scores. Event-derived temporal features such as cadence, stride time, swing time, stance time, temporal asymmetry, double-support overlap, and U-turn duration are traceable to the metadata/events. Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: Clinical Gait Signals dataset paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions

The local gait-analysis source set supports cautious pathology-aware interpretation without making a new diagnosis. In CVA/stroke-labeled cases, reduced speed, shorter steps, and left-right temporal asymmetry are consistent with asymmetric or hemiparetic gait interpretation. In Parkinson disease-labeled cases, short step or stride length with cadence changes can support a short-step Parkinsonian pattern when grounded in the case values. In hip or knee osteoarthritis-labeled cases, slower speed and increased double support can support cautious or load-avoidance interpretation. In neuropathy-labeled cases, variability, asymmetry, and increased support time should be framed as possible stability-control findings rather than proof of sensory loss. | source: Perry & Burnfield plus local pathological-gait reviews summarized in PATHOLOGICAL_GAIT_SOURCE_COVERAGE_2026-06-14.md

Perry and Burnfield describe gait-cycle timing through stance, swing, stride, and double-support intervals. In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (gait cycle, stance, swing, support timing)

Perry and Burnfield frame walking speed, cadence, step length, stride length, and stride timing as linked distance-time gait descriptors. For Data_2, reduced approximate speed together with reduced approximate step or stride length supports an interpretation of reduced forward progression. Cadence should be interpreted with step and stride length: low cadence suggests slower stepping frequency, while high cadence with short steps can indicate a short-step timing strategy. Because Data_2 speed, step length, and stride length are protocol-distance estimates, claims must call them approximate. | source: Perry & Burnfield, Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function (distance-time gait parameters)

In Data_2, toe-off to heel-strike is treated as swing and heel-strike to the next toe-off as stance. Prolonged stance or increased double-support percentage can support a cautious or stability-seeking interpretation. Left-right asymmetry in stride, swing, or stance timing supports an asymmetric temporal gait pattern. Increased stride-time variability supports a less consistent gait-cycle timing interpretation. | source: perry_2010_gait_analysis_normal (local PDF, gait-cycle and stance/swing timing; Data_2 event definitions)

Approximate straight walking speed, step length, and stride length are derived from the protocol distance and event counts, so they must not be presented as true foot-trajectory measurements. | source: clinical_gait_signals_2025 (Clinical Gait Signals paper and bundled plot_data.py event definitions)
